t: Introduction: topic and lecture outline
n: In this lecture we shall consider the bioethical problems associated with the achievements of genetics. Genetics is developing rapidly, but the consequences of applying new achievements in practice may be uncertain or dangerous. The lecture consists of four parts. First we shall look at international documents, then move on to the question of the genome and patents. Next we shall analyse the problem of genetic information, and finally study the history of eugenics.

t: Second half of the 20th century: genomics and proteomics
n: In the second half of the twentieth century the fundamental medical and biological sciences developed rapidly. The study of the structure of the human genome was almost completed. New fields of genetics, namely genomics and proteomics, were discovered and corresponding data banks were established. Hereditary pharmacology emerged, and artificial vaccines are being successfully developed. Remember: genomics and proteomics are not the same thing; they are two separate new fields of genetics.

t: New technologies: uncertainty and risk
n: Many new technologies are associated with uncertainty about the consequences of their use or with the evident danger of their introduction. The modern, genetics-based trend in eugenics envisages the artificial breeding of people with desirable properties and is extremely dangerous socially. At the end of the 1980s the Council of Europe decided to create a document of pan-European significance, because the risk of negative consequences was real. In 1993 the General Assembly adopted the Convention for the protection of human rights and dignity, and the text was approved in November 1996.

t: The specific character of medical genetics ethics
n: The specific character of medical genetics ethics is that hereditary diseases are passed on to descendants. For this reason the problems in this field are not personal but rather family-wide and intergenerational in character. There is no effective method of treating most hereditary diseases, and often only diagnosis and preventive measures remain. Genetic practice is above all care for the health of unborn children, that is, of future generations. Neglecting the interests of future generations is a form of "generational selfishness", but giving them unjustified priority is also contrary to justice.

t: Genetic information and informing relatives
n: Confidentiality and patient autonomy are the basic principle in genetics too. However, the question becomes more complex because genetic information also concerns relatives. In a hereditary disease that threatens life or carries a risk of serious disability, the physician explains to the patient the need to inform relatives. The information given to a relative should be limited only to the part concerning his own likelihood of serious disease. In a complex case, an ethics committee makes the decision. The result of a compulsory genetic examination may become a tool of discrimination by the employer.

t: Council of Europe Convention: timeline
n: Now let us look at the path of the Council of Europe Convention. At the end of the 1980s the risk of negative consequences was real, so the Council of Europe decided to create a pan-European document. In 1993 the General Assembly adopted the convention for the protection of human rights and dignity. After substantial changes were made to the text, it was approved in November 1996 at a session of the Parliamentary Assembly.

t: UNESCO Universal Declaration: history of adoption
n: The UNESCO Universal Declaration was approved by the member states at the UNESCO General Conference on 11 November 1997. In 1998 the declaration was also adopted by the UN General Assembly. In 2000 in Okinawa, the leaders of the Group of Eight, that is, the G-8, endorsed the concept of not deriving income from the genome. Thus the declaration was adopted first at the level of UNESCO, then of the UN, and was then supported by the G-8 leaders.

t: Article 1 of the Declaration: genome and dignity
n: According to Article 1 of the Declaration, the human genome underlies the fundamental unity of all members of the human family, as well as the recognition of their dignity and diversity. The genome expresses human dignity, and the article provides a philosophical basis for the equality and diversity of all people. Humanity has developed for millions of years on the basis of a single set of genes, so the genome of each person is the wealth of all. According to data obtained up to 2001, the genome consists of 30,000 genes. Their variants have formed, and continue to form, people of equal worth.

t: Every genome is the heritage of all humanity
n: The Universal Declaration on the Human Genome and Human Rights was adopted on 11 November 1997. Article 1 links the genome with human dignity. The set of genes has been passed from generation to generation. Nobody knows from whom the genes came a million years ago, or to whom they will pass in a thousand years. For this reason the genome of every person is regarded as the heritage and wealth of the whole of humanity. Article 2 is the logical continuation of Article 1: every individual has the right to respect for his rights and dignity, regardless of genetic characteristics.

t: Article 4: the genome is not a source of income
n: According to Article 4, the human genome in its natural state cannot serve as a source of income. The part of the genome described, that is, discovered, by a researcher is not patented and not turned into a commodity. Remember: describing, that is, discovering, does not mean owning. It is impossible to derive income from the genome in its natural state, to patent a discovered part, or to turn the genome into an object of trade. Free scientific access to the results is nevertheless supported as a principle.

t: The Okinawa meeting and Matsuura's appeal
n: At the meeting in Okinawa in July 2000, the leaders of the world's eight leading countries, that is, the G-8, endorsed this concept. The Director-General of UNESCO, K. Matsuura, sent a letter to the G-8 participants and demanded a statement on the free use by the scientific community of genome research results. According to Matsuura, the principle of free access serves as a guideline for conducting research and applying scientific results while respecting human rights and dignity. This view reflects the position of the UNESCO International Bioethics Committee headed by Professor Ryuichi Ida.

t: Quick question: Articles of the Declaration
n: Let us review the articles of the Declaration. Article 1: the human genome is based on recognition of the unity of all people, their dignity and diversity, and the genome expresses human dignity. Article 2: every individual has the right to respect for his rights and dignity, regardless of genetic characteristics. Article 4: the genome in its natural state cannot be a source of income. Remember: Article 4, that is, no trade. Article 7: genetic data by which a person can be identified must be kept confidential. Remember: Article 7, that is, keeping secrecy.

t: Article 7: confidentiality of genetic data
n: Article 7 is devoted to the confidentiality of genetic data. Genetic data by which a person can be identified must be protected in accordance with the law. This protection applies if the information is stored or processed for scientific or any other purposes. The danger is that if the genome sequence indicates a predisposition to disease, an enterprise may dismiss the person. This is one form of discrimination. Attention: Article 7 requires confidentiality, whereas Article 4 prohibits deriving income from the genome. They are not the same thing.

t: Genome research: human rights and freedom of science
n: Section C considers the rights of two parties: the person examined and the researcher. The person examined may be a patient or a healthy person; his rights, freedom and dignity take precedence over the research. The researcher is a scientist engaged in scientific inquiry; he has the right to pursue science, but this right does not rank above human rights. No genome research may be placed above a person's rights, freedom and dignity. Cloning for the purpose of reproducing a human being is impermissible, but this does not mean a ban on studying the science of cloning.

t: Cloning: what is prohibited and what is not
n: According to the Declaration, cloning for the purpose of reproducing a human being violates human dignity, and therefore it is impermissible. Attention: this prohibition does not mean halting science. Studying scientific work in the field of cloning is not prohibited. Some states have adopted a prohibition law. The USA and Russia, however, declared a five-year moratorium in order to return to the question later.

t: Case analysis 1: the genome and human rights
n: The first case analysis. Situation: a research group has described a fragment of the human genome and wants to patent it and make it an object of commerce. Under Article 4 of the Declaration, the human genome in its natural state cannot be a source of income, so the described part cannot be patented and turned into a commercial object. Article 1 calls the genome an expression of the unity and dignity of humanity. Article 2 recognises every person's right to respect regardless of genetic characteristics. Question: which articles of the Declaration stand in the way of the group's plan, and why? Justify your answer by relying on the content of the articles.

t: Who owns hereditary information?
n: The question arises: who is the owner of hereditary information? The source names four claimants: the person who provided the material, the scientist who described the fragment, the researcher who applied it, and the firm that funded the research. The source gives no definite answer; this question is left open. At the same time, patent applications are very numerous. The growing number of patents is making treatment and genetic tests expensive for most people.

t: Patents and the price dilemma
n: Patents and the price dilemma. Patent applications on genome sequences are very numerous, even though their future benefit is unknown. As patents multiply, treatment and genetic tests are becoming too expensive for most people and countries. Patent protection provides an incentive for income and investment, but the price becomes unattainable for the majority. If protection is narrowed, people will enjoy the fruits of discovery, but investment will fall. The dilemma is whether a discovery should be protected, or whether protection should be narrowed at the risk of reduced investment.

t: AIDS drugs: an example of patent and price
n: Drugs for AIDS, that is, acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, are protected by patent and therefore very expensive in many countries. The conflict between patent and price is not new: it has long been seen precisely in the example of these drugs. Discoveries in genetics extend the scale of this problem still further.

t: Quick question: patent and ownership
n: Let us review two questions. First question: whose property is the genome? According to the source, the genome of each person is the wealth of all, the heritage of the whole of humanity. Second question: how does patenting affect price? As patents multiply, treatment and tests become more expensive. Remember that under Article 4 of the Declaration the human genome in its natural state cannot be a source of income, and the described part cannot be patented.

t: Genetic data banks: ethical aspects
n: The collection, processing, storage and use of genetic information is a field that gives rise to ethical questions. The International Bioethics Committee of UNESCO devoted a separate report to this question. The Committee considered the purpose of collecting information, informing the donor, voluntary and informed consent, confidentiality, and control of subsequent use. In addition, the traditional attitude of a social, religious or ethnic group to the body must be taken into account. Care must be taken when conducting tests that determine kinship.

t: The Human Genome Project: three levels
n: The Human Genome Project, HGP for short, is an international study whose aim is to determine the sequence of DNA nucleotides and to isolate genes. Annas and Elias recommend observing the social and ethical consequences of the project at three levels: the individual and the family, society, and the philosophical understanding of the human being. At the level of the individual and the family there is a natural asymmetry in the ownership of genetic information: parents are included in information about the child's genome, but not the other way round. The concepts of confidentiality and autonomy must now relate not only to the individual but also to the family or to a group of related families.

t: Risk of discrimination: employment and population groups
n: Behind the wide dissemination of genetic data banks lies the risk of various forms of discrimination. If a genome sequence points to an existing or possibly developing disease, a person may be dismissed. Such a danger may arise as a result of an enterprise's policy to combat occupational diseases. In addition, large population groups may also be discriminated against on the basis of the results of genetic research.

t: Genetic screening: erroneous results
n: Screening identifies carriers of genes for serious hereditary diseases among the population. A classic example is screening for phenylketonuria. In a false negative result, the patient is found healthy and does not receive the necessary treatment. In a false positive result, a healthy person is diagnosed as a carrier of a pathological gene. This causes psychological harm to the child and parents and creates a risk of unjustified treatment. The numbers of false negative and false positive results are interrelated: if we reduce one, the other increases.

t: Indigenous peoples, consent and "biopiracy"
n: Several questions are posed using the example of indigenous peoples. Does informed consent acquire meaning among indigenous peoples? In which language is the information necessary for consent given to them? This question also remains open. The community provides genetic material, the research yields a result, and a patent is obtained on the result. The question arises: if the donor community receives no share of the income, would this not be "biopiracy"?

t: Case analysis 2: genetic information and consent
n: The second case analysis. Situation: a genetic sample was taken from a remote community, the research result was patented, but the community received no share of the income. The source calls into question whether such a situation might be "biopiracy", since the donor community is left out of the benefit. There is also the problem of consent: in which language do indigenous peoples receive the necessary information, and does informed consent have meaning for them? To prevent this, the community should take part in the research voluntarily and have full information about it.

t: Genetic engineering: liberal and conservative approaches
n: In bioethical methodology, two approaches to the problems of genetics have emerged: the "liberal" and the "conservative". Supporters of the liberal approach see great prospects in gene therapy and biotechnology, and restrictions seem to them to be a halt to scientific progress. This view is often found among molecular biologists and geneticists and relies on pragmatism and utilitarianism. The conservative view is widespread among lawyers, theologians, some philosophers and scientists.

t: Eugenics: Galton's definition and three stages
n: The term "eugenics" was proposed in 1883 by the English scientist F. Galton. According to Galton's definition, eugenics is the study of the factors that affect the qualities of future generations and require public control. Eugenics passes through three stages: the first is scientific elaboration and propaganda, the second is practical measures and laws, and the third is the stage at which laws become unnecessary. At the last stage laws become unnecessary because people themselves come to understand the necessity of eugenics.

t: Muller's idea and selection criteria
n: Muller, an American scientist, dreamed of populating the Earth with people of genius. He proposed selecting the cleverest people and sterilising the rest, and developed selection criteria. These criteria are giftedness and intellectual capacity, the ability to work together with others, that is, organisation and altruism, and physical and mental health. Attention: the term was introduced by Galton in 1883, whereas Muller is called the "father of eugenics". They are not the same person.

t: Mendel's laws and conclusions about heredity
n: In 1900 the laws of segregation of inborn traits, associated with the name of G. Mendel, were rediscovered. They applied to all plants and animals. Once the chromosome theory of heredity was established, it became clear that the hereditary apparatus is similar in all living beings. This is true for humans too: in families where physical or mental defects have been observed, they are passed from generation to generation. Relying on these theories, far-reaching conclusions about species and races were drawn. However, exaggerating the role of heredity is a mistake.

t: Cultural relativism and polygeny
n: Intellectual ability is not monogenic but polygenic: it is determined by the interaction of several genes. Genes manifest themselves depending on the conditions in which the child grew up and was brought up. Racism holds that races differ in ability, that the only factor is inborn traits, that there are higher and lower races, and its consequence became the basis of fascism. Relativism, on the other hand, says that qualities depend on many factors, that is, on heredity and the cultural environment, and rejects racist ideas. Attention: heredity does not mean destiny.

t: Negative and positive eugenics
n: Negative and positive eugenics: both trends aim to improve heredity, but they differ in method. Negative eugenics relies on prohibitive measures; its means is sterilisation, and its aim is cleansing of harmful hereditary traits. Example: the Indiana law of 1907. Positive eugenics relies on measures of encouragement; its means is selection, and its aim is enrichment with rare hereditary traits. Example: the sperm bank of Nobel laureates. Negative eugenics has a dramatic history: laws on compulsory sterilisation were adopted. Attention: the first prohibits, the second encourages.

t: Quick question: concepts of eugenics
n: Let us review the concepts of eugenics. Galton is the scientist who proposed the term "eugenics" in 1883. Muller, USA, is the "father of eugenics" and a supporter of selecting the cleverest people. Question: which of Muller's criteria is not on the list — giftedness, organisation and altruism, physical and mental health, or wealth? Remember: negative eugenics is prohibition and sterilisation, positive eugenics is encouragement and selection. Attention: monogenic and polygenic differ. Intellectual ability depends not on a single gene but on the interaction of several genes and on the environment of upbringing.

t: Compulsory sterilisation in the USA: dates
n: Compulsory sterilisation in the USA began in 1907 with the Indiana law. In 1924 the law was convenient for northerners and burdensome for the South and East. In 1937 the last compulsory law was issued in Georgia. As a result more than 100 thousand people were sterilised: the mentally ill, the mentally retarded, those convicted of sexual offences, and in some states also alcoholics and orphans. Attention: there was no evidence whatever that those sterilised carried harmful genes. The spread of the idea was helped by the view that immigrants were displacing the "superior" Anglo-Saxons.

t: Germany: racial purity and fascism
n: In Germany, books on "racial purity" spread. In 1933, under Hitler, racism became a state programme. First sterilisation was carried out, then the death camps began, and more than 6 million Jews became victims. At first the mentally ill and mixed-race people born to soldiers of the French army were sterilised. There is information about laws adopted in the Netherlands in the middle of the twentieth century and carried out in secret. The aim was to "cleanse" the population of harmful hereditary traits, and the basis was racist propositions contrary to science.

t: Case analysis 3: eugenics and human rights
n: The third case analysis. Situation: in the USA in 1907 a compulsory sterilisation law was adopted in the state of Indiana. The last such law was issued in 1937 in Georgia. While the laws were in force, more than 100 thousand people, including many African Americans, were forcibly sterilised. In Germany, from 1933, racism became a state programme. First the mentally ill were sterilised, then the death camps began. Question: why did the aim of "cleansing of harmful genes" lead to violations of rights? What evidence concerning those sterilised was lacking?

t: Positive eugenics: banks and ideas
n: Positive eugenics is seen through banks and ideas. Graham established a sperm bank of Nobel laureates, intended for the voluntary insemination of women. Serebrovsky and Muller proposed storing the frozen sperm of donors for insemination. In Muller's opinion, if after a nuclear war men lose the ability to produce offspring, the demand for viable sperm will rise. The table lists the cell banks in the USA: cell and tissue banks, more than 1000; germ cell banks, 343; embryonic cell banks, 200. In 1976 a single association developed common standards for all banks.

t: Ability is polygenic: why "geniuses" cannot be produced
n: Ability is polygenic: it consists of the random crossing of several or many genes, that is, it is not monogenic. In the child of gifted parents, the genes for ability segregate and are dispersed in subsequent generations. Ability is usually not inherited from parents. Every person, even a gifted one, carries a few "harmful" genes in latent form. They may cause serious physical and mental defects. It is not yet possible to determine with 100% certainty whether undesirable genes are present in a genotype. Even if we read the latent information, it is hard to understand it fully.

t: From eugenics to medical genetics
n: The aim that eugenics set, that is, to rid humanity of harmful heredity, now rests with medical genetics. According to Dubinin, medicine weakens the heredity of the species, so the health of the individual and the health of the species are in conflict. The question-and-answer table says that only a universal human approach, not a class or professional one, will accomplish this. The necessary qualities are intelligence, adaptability and health. The main task today is the management of hereditary changes. The adaptive environment consists of climate, diet and medicines. Attention: eugenics is the past, and the aims it set have passed to medical genetics.

t: Prenatal diagnosis: methods and timing
n: In prenatal diagnosis, the traditional method is cytogenetic analysis of the karyotype of cells obtained by amniocentesis; the book gives this as week 13 or 14. The new method was introduced in 1980: trophoblast biopsy and molecular hybridisation, that is, obtaining particles of chorionic villi, make diagnosis possible at weeks 5–6. If a genetic anomaly is found, at weeks 9–10 the question of voluntary termination of pregnancy can be considered. It is indicated that diagnosis before fertilisation to determine embryo quality carries the risk of sliding into eugenics.

t: Conclusion: technology, law and responsibility
n: Let us sum up. The human genome is the heritage of all humanity: in its natural state it cannot be a source of income, and cloning for the purpose of reproducing a human being is prohibited. Genetic data banks create a risk of discrimination, for example dismissal, while patents make treatment and tests more expensive. The lesson of eugenics is that it served to justify compulsory sterilisation and the crimes of racism. Today medical genetics serves quality of life. Topics for independent work: the negative consequences of genetic data banks, the content of informed consent, and why the biotechnological reproduction of a human being is prohibited.
